reasoning: 4-year-old with VP shunt presenting with altered mental status (sleepiness), headache, and nausea—classic triad for shunt malfunction/obstruction
Pediatric vital signs: HR 120 is upper-normal to mildly elevated for age 4 (normal 80–120); RR 22 is at upper limit (normal 20–25); BP 94/76 is low-normal to borderline low for age 4
Altered responsiveness: child is sleepy but arousable to verbal stimuli—meets ESI-2 criterion 'confused/altered mental status' or 'extreme distress'; not fully alert

High-risk condition: VP shunt malfunction is a neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate imaging (CT/ultrasound) and possible neurosurgery intervention; even partial obstruction can progress rapidly to increased intracranial pressure, herniation
Cumulative risk: combination of device-dependent patient + acute neuro symptoms + borderline vital signs in pediatric patient = cannot safely observe; requires urgent evaluation

ESI-2 assignment (not ESI-3) because: (1) altered mental status is a high-risk situation even with stable oxygenation; (2) shunt emergencies are time-sensitive; (3) pediatric compensatory physiology masks severity—child may decompensate rapidly
No immediate life-saving intervention in progress → not ESI-1; but high-risk status with concerning trajectory → ESI-2
red_flags: VP shunt patient with headache and nausea (classic obstruction triad)
Tachycardia (HR 120) and tachypnea (RR 22) may reflect early compensation or ICP rise
Borderline-low BP for age; pediatric patients maintain BP until late decompensation
First-time patient with no baseline for comparison; cannot exclude acute deterioration
Risk of rapid progression to increased ICP, altered consciousness, seizure, or cardiopulmonary compromise
